background.title: Why start from memory
background.html:
Rereading your notes feels like learning because the words look familiar. But in the exam nothing is in front of you. Pulling an idea out of your memory, even slowly and with gaps, makes it much easier to pull out next time.

So today every part starts with a blank page: you write what you remember, then you check. The gaps you find are not a failure; they show exactly what to learn this week.

background.title: One paragraph is not a whole Paper 1 answer
background.html:
In the exam you write a full answer on each text: an introduction, several paragraphs and a conclusion. The examiner marks the whole answer with four criteria, A to D, 5 marks each.

Today you write one paragraph, so you cannot give it a real mark. Instead you use the IB's own words for each level as a mirror: which description sounds most like your paragraph?

background.title: Artificial intelligence in a few lines
background.html:
Artificial intelligence (AI) means computer programs that do things we used to think only people could do: write essays, make pictures, hold a conversation. In 2026 many people use it every day.

People also argue about it: it could be used to cheat, to spread lies or to harm, and it needs huge buildings full of computers (datacentres) that use a lot of electricity and water. Today's cartoon comments on that debate.

background.title: French: a clause or a noun group
background.html:
A clause has a subject and a conjugated verb: ils regardent leur téléphone (they look at their phone).

A noun group is a noun with its little words, and no verb: les écrans, l'arrivée des smartphones.

Some French connectors must be followed by a clause, others by a noun group. Choosing the wrong one is the most common connector mistake.

terms.def: Pulling something out of your memory without looking at notes. It strengthens the memory far more than rereading.
Writing down everything you remember about a topic on a blank page, fast and without notes, before checking.
The tab in your study sheet where you write every lost mark, its type and the rule that fixes it.
The standards your answer is marked against. Paper 1 has four, A to D, each worth 5 marks per text.
Not seen before. In Paper 1 the texts are new to you, so you prepare a method, not answers.
Not a novel, poem or play. Everyday texts such as adverts, speeches, blogs, photographs, infographics and cartoons.
The kind of text, such as an advert, a speech or a cartoon. Each type has its own usual features.
The question printed with each Paper 1 text. It points you to one aspect of how the text works; keep coming back to it.
Your class method for each point: spot a choice, explain it (name the technique), say its effect on the reader, link it to the purpose.
Your class annotation tool: five groups of questions (Audience, Meaning, Feeling, Craft, Shape) to ask about any text.
One box (one picture) on a comic page. A page is usually several panels read in order.
The empty strip between two comic panels. Time passes there, and the reader imagines what happens in it.
In comics, the reader's mind joining separate panels into one story and filling in what is not drawn.
The kind of jump from one panel to the next: a second later, the next action, another person, another time or place.
How close the camera (or artist) is to the subject: from extreme close-up (one detail) to extreme long shot (a tiny figure in a huge place).
How high the camera is compared with the subject: above looking down (high), level (eye level) or below looking up (low).
A line or box of words above, below or inside a picture. In a comic, the narrator's voice; in a cartoon, the line under the picture.
The bubble with a little tail that holds what a character says.
An art word (Italian for "light-dark"): strong contrast between light and dark areas. Say it "kee-ar-oh-SKOO-roh".
How fast or slowly a story seems to move for the reader.
A row of panels read one after the other, telling one small part of the story.
A page layout of panels in regular rows and columns, all about the same size.
Latin for "it does not follow": something with no logical link to what came before.
A picture where the character is tiny in a huge setting, which can show isolation or scale.
Showing an issue as a different, familiar situation, so the reader judges it the same way. Here: the first fire stands for today's AI.
Something placed in the wrong time, such as a modern word or object in a Stone Age scene. Cartoonists use it to make a joke and a point.
The three dots ... at the end of a sentence: it trails off and leaves the reader to finish the thought.
One strong colour against a plain or dull background, so the eye goes straight to it.
Placing two contrasting things side by side so the reader compares them.
Words that mean, or hide, the opposite of what they say: "lovely weather" in a storm.
What a text suggests without saying it directly. You work it out from clues.
Your reasoned idea of what a text means beyond the obvious, supported by details from it.
Judging how well something works, with reasons: is the cartoon effective, and why?
Clear and logical: each sentence follows from the one before, so the whole makes sense as one argument.
Small, less obvious details or meanings that a careful reader notices.
Only saying what is there, without explaining how it creates meaning. The IB marks this low in criterion B.
How formal the language is, and whose kind of voice it sounds like. Exam answers need a formal register.
Write short notes on or next to a text while you study it: circle details, label techniques, jot down ideas.
Verbs that say what a choice does: exposes, ridicules, undermines, invites, positions, implicates, provokes, disarms, reinforces, challenges.
What the creator wants the text to do to its audience: expose, warn, persuade, make them laugh at something.
In satire, the person, group or idea being criticised.
Step 6 of your class revision guide: your own collection of cartoons you have analysed, for revision.
A word or phrase that links ideas, such as parce que (because) or grâce à (thanks to).
A group of words with a subject and a conjugated verb: ils regardent leur téléphone.
A noun with its little words, and no verb: les écrans, l'arrivée des smartphones.
